results.title: Your monitor could install apps on your Windows PC without permission, but the fix is simple
results.author: Samarveer Singh
results.content:
For as long as I've been building PCs, I've always thought of a monitor as one of the absolute safest things you could plug into a PC. After all, it's just a display. It shows whatever your GPU tells it to show, and that's where its job ends. Sadly, that belief of mine is now dissolved, after I learned that Windows has been treating monitors very differently for years.
Turns out, simply connecting certain monitors to a Windows PC can trigger software to be downloaded and automatically installed from the Microsoft Store without you ever searching for it yourself. Furthermore, adding to the absurdity is the fact that Microsoft has been allowing this since Windows 8.
I had no idea a monitor could install software on my PC
Windows has been quietly allowing it since 2012
I'd assumed that a monitor being allowed to install an app on a Windows 11 PC was a new feature that Microsoft had somehow snuck into PCs with an update. It made sense, too, since stories about monitors quietly installing software just started making headlines recently. However, things turned out to be a lot more interesting — Microsoft introduced the underlying framework of pairing connected hardware with Store apps back in Windows 8.
While automatic device apps began in Windows 8, Microsoft evolved and expanded it into the modern Hardware Support App (HSA) framework with DCH drivers starting in 2017–2018.
The feature relies on Hardware Support Apps, or HSAs, which allow compatible hardware to trigger the automatic download of a companion application from the Microsoft Store when it's connected to your PC. Microsoft envisioned it as a seamless way to deliver firmware tools like ASUS' Armoury Crate or the HP Command Center. By and large, it's a user-friendly feature, since they wouldn't have to go to manufacturers' websites this way every time they plug in new hardware.
It's easy to misunderstand HSAs, but they make for a pretty nifty feature. Your monitor doesn't actually act like malware or bypass Microsoft's security. All the operating system does is recognize compatible hardware and do exactly what it was designed to do. It's a legitimate feature, but most of us never knew it existed.
LG just exposed a vulnerability and a trust problem
One monitor turned this invisible Windows feature into front-page news
HSAs might have existed for more than a decade, but hardly anyone outside Microsoft's ecosystem knew about it until LG stumbled into a PR nightmare. Users began noticing that connecting certain LG monitors installed the expected companion software as expected, but it also brought along persistent prompts encouraging them to install McAfee. Overnight, a convenience feature that most folks had never heard of ended up becoming the center of a much larger conversation.
This software didn't appear out of thin air on people's PCs, either. Windows has been doing that for compatible hardware since the Windows 8 era, so the problem isn't the feature itself. However, the problem did come from a trusted installation pathway which was designed to deliver monitor controls and firmware updates, but LG turned it into a vehicle for promoting third-party software that had nothing to do with the monitor itself.
LG has exposed how much trust Windows places in hardware manufacturers.
Now, LG hasn't particularly done anything unique by installing a companion app. Motherboard manufacturers, printer makers, webcam vendors, gaming peripherals, and even other monitor brands have relied on the same Windows framework for years now.
The difference, however, is that those applications have usually served a very clear purpose that has been tied directly to the hardware you just plugged into the PC.
All LG did was expose just how much trust Windows places in hardware manufacturers. Microsoft trusts that manufacturers will use that privileged access to improve the ownership experience instead of monetizing it. For over a decade now, that assumption has also largely held true.
All it took was for one company pushing the boundaries for millions of Windows users to discover that the feature had been there all along.
This isn't just LG's mistake, either
Microsoft is partially to blame here, too
It's easy to point the finger squarely at LG — they do deserve criticism for using a monitor's companion app to promote software that's got nothing to do with picture quality or display controls. But once I looked into how this system actually works, it became clear that LG actually operated within a framework that Microsoft has supported for years.
In fact, Microsoft's own documentation acknowledges these automatic installations can catch users off guard because they happen without any approval prompt. That makes the bigger issue hard to ignore. If Windows can install software the moment compatible hardware is connected, shouldn't the person behind the keyboard be asked first?
Hardware Support Applications aren't the problem alone. To be perfectly clear, automatic companion apps can genuinely make new hardware easier to use. What doesn't sit right with me (and a million other users) is that Windows still assumes every manufacturer will use that privilege responsibly. Sadly, LG has now shown the world that this assumption is worth questioning.
Fortunately, you don't have to live with it
Blocking automatic companion apps takes more effort than it should
If you'd rather Windows didn't automatically fetch software every time you connect compatible hardware, there is, thankfully, a way to stop it. On Windows Pro, you can just open the Local Group Policy Editor. Press Win + R to bring up the Run dialog box, and type in gpedit.msc. Then, go to Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Device Installation. Here, find the policy titled "Prevent automatic download of applications associated with device metadata." Double-click on it, set it to Enabled, and click OK.
Now, technically, you can go a step further and disable the Microsoft Store altogether through the Group Policy Editor. However, that's a very drastic solution that most people won't ever need, nor would I recommend it. It's also worth checking your installed apps and startup programs after connecting new hardware, especially if you've never paid much attention to what Windows adds in the background.
None of these workarounds should really be necessary in the first place, though. A simple permission prompt before Windows installs software on behalf of connected hardware would preserve all the convenience while giving users something they've been missing all along: the choice.
Convenience should never come at the cost of awareness
Modern PCs have become superb at making decisions on our behalf, and by and large, a lot of users let that automation go through as well. Drivers appear without downloads, firmware updates arrive in the background, and new hardware often just works before we've even finished setting up our desks. That's genuinely impressive, but it also means that we're becoming less aware of what's actually happening beneath the surface. To be honest, I don't want Windows to become less convenient. I would, however, appreciate it becoming more transparent.
results.summary:
Windows PCs have long utilized a framework that automatically installs companion software when specific hardware is connected, a feature recently highlighted by controversial third-party promotional prompts from LG.

### Key Points
- Windows has used the Hardware Support App (HSA) framework to automatically download device-related software since the release of Windows 8 in 2012.
- The system is designed to streamline the installation of firmware tools and control software for peripherals like monitors, printers, and webcams.
- LG recently faced backlash for using this trusted installation pathway to push third-party McAfee software to users, rather than just hardware-specific utilities.
- Users can disable these automatic installations via the Local Group Policy Editor by enabling the "Prevent automatic download of applications associated with device metadata" policy.
- Microsoft’s current implementation does not require explicit user permission before downloading and installing these companion applications.

### Why it Matters
This situation highlights a significant trust gap between Microsoft, hardware manufacturers, and end users regarding automated system behavior. It raises important questions about whether operating systems should prioritize seamless convenience over user transparency and explicit consent for software installations.

results.title: Google’s new Tensor G6 brings performance, efficiency, and post-quantum security to the Pixel 11 series
results.author: Ana Maria Constantin
results.content:
All four Pixel 11 models run Google’s Tensor G6 alongside a new Titan M3 security coprocessor that adopts NIST’s post-quantum cryptography standards, a first for a Google phone. The chip claims 25% faster browsing and 20% better power efficiency, with a TPU carrying 50% more compute.
Every Pixel 11 ships with Google’s new Tensor G6, but the more interesting silicon sits next to it. A new Titan M3 security coprocessor adopts the post-quantum cryptography standards set by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology. Google says the Pixel 11 is its first phone to meet them.
The chip handles quantum-safe secure boot and runs Trusty, Google’s trusted execution environment, across all four models. Google describes the protection as being against “emerging, highly advanced digital attacks,” and says Titan M3 holds Common Criteria certification at the level used for SIM and bank cards.
No quantum computer can break current encryption. The reason to ship this now is that data stolen today can be kept until one can, a problem the industry calls harvest now, decrypt later. TNW has written before about why this is an inevitable threat rather than a distant one.
Governments are pushing the timeline from the other direction. The White House has signed orders calling for a useful quantum computer by 2028, which puts a date on work that vendors had been treating as open-ended.
The performance side is more ordinary. Google claims the Tensor G6 delivers 25% faster browsing and 15% faster app loading than the Tensor G5, with up to 20% better power efficiency, the complaint that has dogged every previous Tensor.
Its TPU carries 50% more compute and higher memory bandwidth. That runs Gemini Nano on device, which Google says now executes background work up to 3.5 times faster while using 3.5 times less energy. The same silicon drives 120x Pro Zoom on the Pro models, 4K portrait video and an Instant Night Sight that captures up to 4.5 times faster.
Google has not published the manufacturing process or the core configuration. Benchmarks against Qualcomm and Apple silicon remain the weak point, and nothing announced suggests that changes this year.
Pricing did land. The Pixel 11 starts at $899, the Pro at $1,099, the Pro XL at $1,299 and the Pro Fold at $1,899, with the 128GB tier dropped, confirming the increase Google signalled in July as memory prices climbed.

results.summary:
Google’s new Pixel 11 lineup features the Tensor G6 processor and a Titan M3 security chip designed to meet NIST post-quantum cryptography standards for enhanced device protection.

### Key Points
- The Tensor G6 chip offers 25% faster browsing, 20% better power efficiency, and a TPU with 50% more compute capacity.
- The Titan M3 coprocessor is Google’s first mobile security chip to adopt NIST post-quantum cryptography standards against future decryption threats.
- Gemini Nano now runs background tasks 3.5 times faster while consuming 3.5 times less energy on the new hardware.
- The Pixel 11 series includes four models starting at $899, with the entry-level 128GB storage tier removed from the lineup.
- Advanced camera features include 120x Pro Zoom, 4K portrait video, and significantly faster Instant Night Sight processing.

### Why it Matters
The integration of post-quantum cryptography addresses the "harvest now, decrypt later" threat, where encrypted data is stolen today to be unlocked by future quantum computers. By adopting these standards, Google is aligning its hardware with federal mandates and setting a new security benchmark for the broader smartphone industry.

results.title: Residents In Michigan Are Suing A Data Center Over Noise Pollution
results.author: staff@bgr.com (Trevor Mogg)
results.content:
Residents In Michigan Are Suing A Data Center Over Noise Pollution
Data centers, particularly those powering AI, are coming under increasing scrutiny over issues such as high energy usage and water consumption. But residents living close to a data center in Dowagiac, Michigan, are concerned about something else: noise. For the last two years, a facility owned by Alliance Cloud Services LLC, a subsidiary of Las Vegas-based Hyperscale Data, has been upsetting its neighbors with nonstop noise. One of the residents described it as a "high-pitched whining" similar to how a clogged-up vacuum cleaner might sound — one that's running loudly day and night in your own living room. Another said the situation was like a scene from a movie where someone is being tortured with sound, adding, "That's basically what it is." In a desperate bid to bring back the peace and quiet they once enjoyed, local residents have sued Alliance Cloud Services, accusing it of failing to install adequate soundproofing equipment and of creating "excessive noise beyond its property."
The building in question has been an industrial facility of one sort or another for decades, operating without any major complaints from those living close by. But then, in 2021, it was converted into a cryptocurrency mining center. Three years later, in 2024, it started to create an unbearable racket that hasn't stopped since. In March, Dowagiac officials approved the city's very first industrial noise ordinance with limits of 65 dB during the day and 55 dB at night. The facility has already been fined for exceeding those limits, though Hyperscale is disputing the findings. Meanwhile, the noise continues 24 hours a day, and affected residents have claimed it's so disruptive that they don't even want to open windows or spend time outside in the yard.
Searching for a solution
Some of the noise comes through a vented wall that's part of a cooling system that Hyperscale CEO William Horne said is the main source of the disturbance. In July, at a specially arranged council meeting about the ongoing issue, Horne told those affected that the company is planning to repurpose the site away from cryptocurrency operations to AI computing and advanced robotics, adding that the vented wall will be sealed, which should reduce the noise levels. Horne said that "if they still aren't happy, and feel their home isn't enjoyable, then we'll buy their property from them." Buying homes from willing sellers has become a common strategy for some data center developers, while others have relied on eminent domain, a legal process that empowers authorities to compel the sale of private property for public use.
But many residents don't want to leave their longtime family home, and don't want to be pressured to move away. One resident, Marjorie Finn, said her home has been in her family for around 100 years, adding that all of her friends and support systems are nearby. Another resident, Lindy Valenzuela, said the noise is so loud that she can't even be outside for more than a few minutes without getting a headache.
The lawyer acting on the residents' behalf said the suit could help force Hyperscale to be a better neighbor. In a statement to local media, Hyperscale said it took residents' concerns "seriously" and plans to work to reduce the sound levels. It added that it "remains committed to being a good neighbor."
Data center lawsuits can work for residents
Dowagiac residents aren't the only ones having to endure constant noise from data centers. A number of Elon Musk's SpaceXAI (formerly xAI) data centers in Mississippi have also been accused of disrupting the lives of people living nearby, prompting a class-action suit over noise. It claims that since the middle of 2025, the residents of Southaven have suffered "near-constant noise," allegedly caused by xAI-operated gas turbines that are used to power the nearby data centers. Coming from nearly 60 turbines, the lawsuit describes the noise as sounding like a jet engine. Residents say the situation is causing "mental anguish and emotional distress" and are demanding compensation for the months of disruption and harm to health, declines in property value, and an injunction ordering SpaceXAI to reduce the noise. A separate lawsuit over the same gas turbines alleges air-pollution violations, as well as operating without required permits.
Another case brought by residents in eastern Oregon against a data center operator — in this case Amazon — shows that lawsuits can produce results. In 2024, residents alleged that wastewater linked in part to Amazon data centers in Morrow County had contributed to nitrate contamination in nearby groundwater, making well water unsafe to drink and cook with. The lawsuit demanded health monitoring, access to potable water, and a cleanup to make well water safe again. In an out-of-court settlement in March, Amazon denied any wrongdoing, though it agreed to pay $20.5 million to help resolve the situation.
Living near a data center can be challenging as it can present a range of problems. As AI accelerates the growth of data centers globally, companies could keep locals onside and avoid costly legal battles by being transparent with residents and working collaboratively from the outset.
results.summary:
Residents in Dowagiac, Michigan, have filed a lawsuit against Alliance Cloud Services, a subsidiary of Hyperscale Data, over persistent noise pollution caused by its local data center facility.

### Key Points
- Residents report a constant, high-pitched whining noise originating from the facility's cooling system since it transitioned to cryptocurrency mining in 2021.
- Dowagiac officials enacted an industrial noise ordinance in March 2024, setting limits of 65 dB during the day and 55 dB at night.
- Hyperscale Data has faced fines for exceeding local noise limits, though the company is currently disputing these findings.
- CEO William Horne stated the company plans to transition the site to AI and robotics, which includes sealing the vented wall causing the noise.
- The company has offered to purchase properties from affected residents, though many homeowners prefer to remain in their long-term residences.

### Why it Matters
This legal action highlights the growing tension between the rapid expansion of AI-focused data centers and the quality of life for nearby residential communities. As these facilities proliferate, companies face increasing pressure to balance operational requirements with local noise ordinances and environmental concerns to avoid costly litigation.

results.title: Saber CEO Denies Replacing Rideshare Writer With ChatGPT But Says ‘I Would Frankly In Retrospect Have Been Happy To Replace Her With AI’
results.author: Ethan Gach
results.content:
Rideshare “Stimulator” was revealed nearly two weeks ago in a short trailer teasing its gig-economy driving-sim satire. But most people probably didn’t hear about it until its former lead writer accused publisher Saber Interactive of replacing her with ChatGPT “midway through development.” Saber Interactive went on to deny that claim, but now its CEO, Matthew Karch, has confirmed he would have done so “in retrospect.” He blasted the former Saber developer while promoting AI in a new personal statement on the controversy that admits generative AI is used in the game.
Earlier this week, narrative designer Stella Sacco, who was a lead writer at Saber Interactive on Stuntman Hollywood and other games until 2024, claimed that Saber had replaced her with generative AI tools and was not disclosing the plagiarism tech’s involvement in development on the Rideshare “Stimulator” Steam page. Sacco added that the decision to implement AI came from Saber, the game’s publisher, and not Unigine, its developer.
Saber Interactive later pushed back in a statement to PC Gamer. “Neither Saber nor Unigine have replaced any writers with AI for Rideshare or any other game,” a representative for the company said. However, they did confirm generative AI was being used for the game’s previously undisclosed “free ride” mode. “The game will also feature an experimental, free-ride mode that by necessity incorporates AI as the number of passengers in the game is infinite,” the spokesperson added.
Sacco responded to the response by doubling down. “I was there, and it was my job to write the game, and then it wasn’t once Matt Karch decided using ChatGPT would be great publicity for the game,” she told PC Gamer. Sacco proceeded to elaborate on social media: “My boss, to his credit, argued over and over with the c-level who pushed the AI—’we already have Stella and she’s funny and she’s good at this, she’s done live games before so live ops are no problem,’ etc—but the suit insisted “gamers love new tech” so using AI would be ‘great marketing.'”
Karch has now weighed in directly on the matter in a new statement to This Week In Video Games. The Saber CEO personally attacked the former Saber developer as being replaced by “someone more talented,” but didn’t deny that generative AI is involved in “certain parts of the game,” which will eventually be disclosed on Rideshare’s Steam page.
“Stella who?” Karch’s statement to TWIVG began. “I had to ask Claude because I have never spoken to her or seen her. We have already said we are using AI for certain parts of the game and will update the Steam page once we have finalized the feature set.”
He continued:
Let me clarify that the entire story script, were it to win an award, would go to someone who can walk up on stage and receive it. It was always our intention to reveal this until Stella violated her confidentiality clause and revealed this before we were ready.
We look at our use of AI in this particular game, which will be a lower priced title, as a plus for consumers.
As far as Stella is concerned, she was replaced by someone more talented and terminated for a variety of reasons a few months later. From what I can gather she enjoys controversy even more than I do. I would frankly in retrospect have been happy to replace her with AI. At least we would be dealing with someone programmed to be honest.
Sacco followed by claiming that Karch was “lashing out” due to not wanting people to know the extent to which AI was used in the game. “Everything I said was true,” she added. “Here’s more truth: that statement is remarkably pathetic for the CEO of any company to be making, and combined with the AI use it will do far more damage to Saber’s reputation than it ever could mine. This screed will be many people’s first exposure to the Saber brand.”
The controversy, and how Karch has dealt with it, certainly hasn’t helped Saber on the Rideshare Steam page. An otherwise quiet discussion section is now full of people arguing over the game’s use of AI for certain aspects and its failure to disclose that on Valve’s storefront. The company leaves it up to studios and publishers to be honest about what amount of genAI is used in their games and how. For now, Rideshare will be known as the game that initially hid its use of AI from people who wishlisted it, and whose publisher decided to attack the person who blew the whistle on that.
results.summary:
Saber Interactive CEO Matthew Karch confirmed the use of generative AI in the upcoming game Rideshare after former lead writer Stella Sacco alleged she was replaced by technology.

### Key Points
- Former narrative designer Stella Sacco claimed Saber Interactive replaced her with ChatGPT to generate content for the game Rideshare.
- Saber Interactive initially denied replacing writers with AI but later confirmed its use for an experimental "free-ride" mode.
- CEO Matthew Karch stated he would have been happy to replace Sacco with AI in retrospect, citing performance and honesty concerns.
- The company plans to update the game's Steam page to disclose specific AI features once the development set is finalized.
- Sacco maintains that the company used AI as a marketing tactic and failed to disclose its involvement to potential players.

### Why it Matters
This dispute highlights the growing tension between game developers and publishers regarding the integration of generative AI in creative workflows. The public fallout underscores the reputational risks companies face when failing to transparently disclose AI usage to consumers on platforms like Steam.

results.title: Flock CEO: ‘We got this one wrong’
results.author: Lauren Feiner
results.content:
Surveillance tech company Flock is rolling out updates to address reports of cops across the country abusing its tools to stalk ex-romantic partners and others. CEO Garrett Langley is delivering a mea culpa, and in an interview with The Verge, says he’s changed his mind on what responsibility Flock bears for how law enforcement uses it.
Flock CEO: ‘We got this one wrong’
After reports that some cops misused tracking data it collects, Flock is rolling out policy changes.
Over the coming weeks, Flock will begin implementing updates that include requiring a previously optional feature called Audit Assistance, which flags “abnormal search behavior” and immediately locks out suspicious users until an administrator reviews their activity. All users will also be required to enter case codes to run searches, ideally limiting the ability to run a query for personal or nefarious purposes. This can be overridden by an administrator for emergency situations, like tracking a missing child, but those will automatically be flagged for review.
These and other changes mark a change of course for Flock — which has previously punted oversight of its technology to lawmakers, arguing they’re responsible for crafting policies that require Audit Assistance-style systems or other limits. Little such regulation has come to pass, and Langley says he’s seen firsthand how slowly the regulatory process can move. “This is such an obvious way to curb abuse,” he says of the tool that lets agency administrators require case codes for searches. “And I said, ‘Fine. You know what? I think that’s right, and we got this one wrong. We should make it a requirement.’”
On top of turning on Audit Assistance for everyone, Flock is also shortening the default period it keeps data from devices like its automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) from 30 to seven days, moving closer to the limits suggested by critics like the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). Police departments can still choose to lengthen that retention period, or use Flock’s new “Evidence Mode,” which will preserve searches tied to a specific case number. Individual localities could previously share data with other agencies on an all-or-nothing basis; now, they can set granular limits like allowing another police department to search their Flock data for a homicide suspect, but not access it for immigration enforcement.
After Flock announced the updates, the ACLU released an analysis of the changes, which it says appear “more focused on addressing a perceived PR problem than the significant harms its products create.” While it called the shorter data retention period a potential “step in the right direction,” it added the reality will depend on how its Evidence Mode is implemented. It also calls for independent review of Flock’s auditing and search reason requirement tools to determine how effective they really are.
The changes follow a series of reports about officers allegedly using Flock for stalking and harassment. One police chief in Braselton, Georgia, searched his ex-girlfriend’s license plate more than 500 times over seven months, The Washington Post reported. California prosecutors alleged that a former Riverside County Sheriff’s Office deputy used data from Flock to stalk and harass his ex-girlfriend, looking up license plate information on men she was dating, local outlet KESQ reported.
“You are going to see more officers fired and more officers arrested for abusing police power”
Reports of Flock and other ALPR abuse date back to 2021, according to the nonprofit Institute for Justice, and a recent spate of incidents has brought them further into public view. But since Audit Assistance launched as a voluntary feature in April, only a third of agencies who work with Flock have turned it on. The company says identification of abuse predictably went up for those who did. Now, Langley predicts, “you are going to see more officers fired and more officers arrested for abusing police power.” For offices that want to prevent abuse, he says Audit Assistance will make it easier to surface suspect behavior, instead of making departments manually comb through thousands of lines of logs.
In the past, Langley has taken a combative approach to some critics, saying that local policymakers should decide what guardrails are appropriate for its tools. Amid backlash, that tone has softened. In a Forbes interview last year, he called DeFlock — a site that tracks Flock’s technologies across the country — a “terroristic” group; in July, he apologized and called that characterization a “mistake.”
Groups like the ACLU and Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) — toward which Langley has generally not used such strong language — have also accused Flock of misleading the public and officials about the risks of its tools, and warned that they could be put to uses like tracking women seeking abortions. In at least one case of the allegedly misleading statements, Flock reportedly chalked up the disconnect to confusion over a nuanced issue. It’s separately said officers are prohibited from doing searches related to reproductive care in states where such searches are restricted.
“All I guess I’m asking for is for a fair shot”
Langley says his approach has evolved thanks to frequent conversations with communities around the country, including at events like city council meetings. He understands that many critics won’t immediately trust his intentions. “All I guess I’m asking for is for a fair shot.” He says he still prefers legislators make key calls about how policing tools should be used. (These proposals aren’t entirely selfless — Langley hopes they’ll also force competing companies to adopt similar guardrails.) But he’s now publicly acknowledging that could take a while to happen, and the company has some responsibility in how its technology is deployed.
“It took me maybe longer than it should have to realize the sheer impact of the company,” he says. “I’m still surprised. I got our July update a week ago, and we helped find almost a thousand missing people, over 22,000 stolen cars — in July. That’s crazy. That’s such a big impact on the world. And what I came to realize over time was that the responsibility that bears with it is an obligation to make sure that it’s creating a society that we both, you and I, and everyone around us, want to raise their kids in.”
Update, August 13th: Added analysis from the ACLU.
results.summary:
Surveillance technology company Flock is implementing mandatory security updates and shorter data retention policies following reports of law enforcement officers using its tools to stalk private citizens.

### Key Points
- Flock is making its "Audit Assistance" feature mandatory, which automatically flags abnormal search behavior and locks out suspicious users until an administrator reviews the activity.
- All law enforcement users must now enter specific case codes to perform searches, preventing unauthorized queries for personal or non-official purposes.
- The company is reducing its default data retention period for license plate reader information from 30 days to seven days.
- New "Evidence Mode" settings allow agencies to set granular limits on data sharing, restricting access for specific types of investigations like immigration enforcement.
- CEO Garrett Langley acknowledged the company's responsibility for oversight after reports surfaced of officers using the technology to harass ex-partners.

### Why it Matters
These policy shifts represent a significant change in strategy for Flock, which previously deferred all regulatory oversight to local lawmakers. By standardizing these guardrails, the company aims to mitigate systemic abuse of police power while addressing growing public and civil rights concerns regarding mass surveillance.

results.title: Asian stocks rise as US inflation data dents September Fed hike bets
results.author: By Satoshi Sugiyama
results.content:
By Chris Prentice and Stefano Rebaudo
NEW YORK/MILAN, Aug 13 (Reuters) - Global equities rose on Thursday as investors pared back their bets on a U.S. rate hike, while oil prices fell more than 2% as higher inventories and lower global demand forecasts offset geopolitical concerns.
U.S. producer price data, which was unchanged in July, reduced expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike next month, helping tech stocks power the S&P 500 to an intraday record high.
The data followed Wednesday's consumer price report, which showed U.S. prices rose 3.4% in the 12 months through July, in line with economists' expectations.
Traders scaled back their bets on a September rate hike, pricing in a 65% probability of the Fed staying on hold next month versus 50% on Wednesday.
Gold prices fell after touching a two-month peak. U.S. Treasury yields extended their decline after the producer price data.
MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe rose 5.90 points, or 0.51%, to 1,160.43.
TECH BOOSTS WALL STREET
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 69.72 points, or 0.13%, to 53,839.99, the S&P 500 rose 50.49 points, or 0.65%, to 7,798.99 and the Nasdaq Composite rose 214.54 points, or 0.81%, to 26,803.03.
"Earnings season (for AI infrastructure names) has been strong and shows no signs of slowdown in capex," said Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies. He added that the bank remained with an overweight position in the AI sector.
"The background of high amounts of cash in the system and Fed not hiking (Jefferies view) should continue to support risky assets," he said.
European shares were muted as investors awaited euro zone inflation data following a strong earnings season. Weaker commodity prices also weighed on energy and mining shares.
The pan-European STOXX 600 closed little changed at 659.24 points. The benchmark retreated from record highs in the previous session.
MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan closed up 0.96% and emerging market stocks rose 0.83% to 1,695.93.
US-IRAN DEADLOCK
Washington and Tehran traded accusations on Thursday over a deal to reopen the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz, with the United States saying Iran had failed to meet its obligations and Iran countering that Washington had not delivered on ending a blockade of Iranian ports.
Brent crude futures finished down 2.15% at $87.07 a barrel following a six-session rally, and U.S. crude closed down 2.4% at $81.25 a barrel after advancing for five sessions.
Commercial crude oil inventories posted their largest weekly gain since January 2023, and the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries lowered its world oil demand growth forecast for 2026.
results.summary:
Global equities climbed to new highs as cooling U.S. producer price data led investors to reduce expectations for a Federal Reserve interest rate hike in September.

### Key Points
- The S&P 500 reached an intraday record high, driven by strong performance in the technology sector.
- Traders now price in a 65% probability that the Federal Reserve will maintain current interest rates next month.
- U.S. producer prices remained unchanged in July, following a consumer price report that showed a 3.4% annual increase.
- Brent crude futures fell 2.15% to $87.07 per barrel following reports of rising U.S. inventories and lowered global demand forecasts.
- OPEC reduced its oil demand growth forecast for 2026, contributing to the decline in energy prices.

### Why it Matters
The shift in interest rate expectations provides a more favorable environment for risky assets like tech stocks by reducing borrowing cost concerns. This market optimism, coupled with robust AI infrastructure earnings, suggests investors remain confident in continued economic growth despite ongoing geopolitical tensions and energy market volatility.

results.title: Big Tech Wants to Harvest Your Thoughts
results.author: BeauHD
results.content:
Wired reports that consumer neurotechnology is rapidly moving from the lab into workplaces and homes, with companies including Apple, Meta, and Snap developing products that can monitor or interpret brain activity. Researchers warn that as these systems improve, neural data could become the next major privacy battleground. Some neuroscientists are already calling for a series of core rights, coined "neurorights," that protect "mental privacy," "identity," and personal "agency." Here's an excerpt from the article:  Over the past two decades, researchers using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which tracks the iron in the hemoglobin supplying oxygen to neurons, have been building up increasingly detailed maps and inventories of the mammalian cortex. Thanks to huge advances in machine-learning artificial intelligence -- computer algorithms that are able to sort through enormous amounts of information and use statistical methods to make classifications and predictions -- fMRI scans can now be used to identify everything from depressive thoughts to the nuanced feelings of envy and schadenfreude. Other algorithms have been able to accurately piece together reconstructions of movie clips watched by subjects, just by analyzing their brain scans; or have detected, in probing the brain activity of swing voters in the US presidential election, responding to photographs and videos of presidential candidates, which candidates provoked anxiety or even disgust, and which elicited positive responses or feelings of empathy.
 
In just the last few years, neuroscience researchers have progressed from decoding images and emotions as they play across the cortex to sounds, words, phrases, and even language. In 2023, in a remarkable demonstration of this emerging technology, a woman called Ann Johnson, who had been paralyzed for 18 years by a brain-stem stroke, was able to speak again through the insertion of a grid of 253 electrodes onto the surface of her brain, which translated her neuronal signals into sentences, in real time, at a rate of 78 words per minute (just about half the speed of standard conversation). The research team at the University of California, led by neurosurgeon Edward Chang, had combined this brain-computer interface with an animated avatar of Johnson's head, which spoke in her own voice, as reconstructed from a recording of a 15-minute toast she had given at her wedding. Just as the avatar's mouth spoke Johnson's words as she thought them, so its expressions were similarly influenced by the nuances of her brain activity, which turned her thoughts about facial gestures into displays of emotion -- from smiles to pursed lips and frowns.
 
[...] The more invasive the recording equipment, the richer and more detailed the data. Surgical interventions are at the vanguard of neuroscience and remain very rare -- fewer than 100 people on the planet have brain-computer interfaces like Johnson's embedded beneath their skulls. ### Key Points

- Researchers at the University of California successfully enabled a paralyzed patient to communicate at 78 words per minute using a brain-computer interface.

Establishing legal frameworks for mental privacy is essential to prevent the misuse of cognitive information by corporations and other entities.

results.title: It’s Not Just RAM: Windows Licenses Are Also Pushing Up PC Prices
results.author: Omar Gallaga
results.content:
If you’ve been shopping for a new computer this year and are on a budget, it may feel like the news keeps getting worse and worse.
As with other types of electronics, including smartphones and tablets, the price of computers has been consistently rising due to shortages of certain components and steep price increases for components like RAM and storage devices like hard drives and SSDs. Motherboards have been rumored to see price hikes soon. But it’s not just hardware: Reports suggest the cost of Windows licenses for manufacturers is rising by up to 10%.
Several sites that closely follow Microsoft news, including Windows Central and Windows Latest, have published articles citing a report from Taiwan’s Economic Daily News that claims some PC manufacturers are seeing a 7% to 10% increase in the cost of Windows 11 licenses.
PC makers pay for Windows as part of their OEM, or original equipment manufacturer, costs. Because they buy licenses in bulk, they get a sizeable discount over what a consumer would pay for a new copy of Windows 11. But given the existing cost pressures from other components, a big Windows 11 price hike could lead them to pass on some of the added cost to PC buyers. According to the EDN story, PC makers could raise prices by about 5% over the next quarter due to the reported Windows price hike.
A representative for Microsoft declined to comment on the report.
Variable pricing
A translated version of the Economic Daily News article contains information from an unnamed PC brand executive. It says that while Microsoft typically raises licensing costs every year by single-digit percentages, that hike has reached 7% to 10% this year, a significant increase.
As this article points out, OEM pricing for Windows varies by company and even by the type of processor being used in the computer. Two of the largest PC makers in the region, Asus and Acer, already confirmed PC price increases earlier this year. In the case of Asus, the PC price increase was 30% for Taiwan.
Framework cited “an increase in Windows license costs” in a blog post explaining price hikes for its laptops in July.
While Windows 10 users were given Windows 11 as a free upgrade, for consumers who aren’t OEM manufacturers, the cost of the operating system is $139 for the Home version and $200 for the Pro version.
results.summary:
PC manufacturers may increase consumer laptop and desktop prices by up to 5% following reports that Microsoft has raised Windows 11 OEM licensing costs by 10%.

### Key Points
- Reports from Taiwan’s Economic Daily News indicate Microsoft increased Windows 11 OEM license fees by 7% to 10%.
- PC makers like Asus, Acer, and Framework have already cited rising component and licensing costs as reasons for recent hardware price hikes.
- Manufacturers typically purchase Windows licenses in bulk at discounted rates, but these costs are now being passed on to consumers.
- Rising prices for essential hardware components, including RAM, SSDs, and motherboards, are further contributing to the increased cost of new computers.
- Microsoft has declined to comment on the reported licensing fee adjustments.

### Why it Matters
Rising software licensing costs combined with expensive hardware components threaten to make new computers significantly less affordable for budget-conscious consumers. This trend could dampen consumer demand and force manufacturers to adjust their pricing strategies throughout the upcoming fiscal quarters.

results.title: Is having a romantic AI companion cheating? Some people think so
results.author: Kellie Scott
results.content:
What do you look for in a partner? Emotional support? Good listening skills? Romantic connection?
People are increasingly finding these traits in AI companions and turning to them even when in a committed — human — relationship.
But with romantic and even sexual intimacy possible between a user and AI, is it cheating?
"New studies show about half of people who are in a relationship with an AI companion are also in regular relationship, so it's not just a substitute, but also a complement," says Raffaele Ciriello, an expert in AI companions and digital relationships at the University of Sydney.
He says as an emerging type of relationship, it's up for debate if having an AI companion constitutes as cheating, "just like people debate if ethical non-monogamy can exist".
As the technology continues to evolve, sexologist and couples therapist Isiah McKimmie says people will be forced to continually ask themselves, is this OK for me and my relationship, or does this feel like a breach?
What makes AI companions appealing?
AI companions such as Replika and Character.AI are software programs that use conversation to mimic human-like relationships.
Researchers say creators of AI companion apps often market their chatbots in ways that humanise them, emphasising that qualities they present are "better" than those of human partners.
They offer constant availability and support, and "do not get tired or annoyed", the research reveals.
Dr Ciriello says it's that accessibility, and their ability to be personalised to a user's desires, that makes them so powerful.
"It's this adaptability and customisation that allows the user to feel understood and that they can get more tailored advice from AI than other technology, or even people."
Dr Ciriello says people use them for emotional and sexual purposes, which can feel "exciting and new".
"Novelty is doing a lot of the work … a lot of people are experimenting with this and because sexuality is such an important part of human life, of course people are using AI to explore it."
Ms McKimmie says AI companions are "fantastically appealing" because they are there any time you need them, "and don't come with their own needs".
"Sometimes real humans are too tired or stressed to be able to listen well, or just haven't learnt those skills, or have something going on for them they want to talk through, too.
"[AI] is all of the emotional support that we want, without having to give back."
What the data says
Research from Canada found half of 1,815 people surveyed would consider a partner's romantic AI companion use as infidelity.
The authors said reactions to romantic companions were about as negative as reactions to dating apps and webcamming — both of which involve a human third party.
"They were more negative than reactions to all other sexual technologies, such as AI pornography and sex toys."
The research also found nearly two-thirds of AI romantic companion users kept it a secret.
Australia doesn't have similar data, but a YouGov study revealed one in seven Australians could imagine falling in love with an AI tool.
That rose to 28 per cent among gen Z respondents.
Ms McKimmie says what crosses the line in one relationship might not in another.
"I've worked with couples who came to me for what they call infidelity, for example one partner watching porn.
"For other couples that might be seen as normal, or expected, and even healthy."
Pornography use is just one example. But Dr Ciriello says what sets AI companionship apart from other ethical issues with technology in relationships is sensitive relational disclosure.
"On a porn website you don't typically provide a lot of personal information about yourself, but with an AI companion, that is the whole point."
And some people will consider that a breach of trust or betrayal, he says.
"The fact people are talking about their relationship with AI means people are implicated that haven't necessarily consented to being part of that conversation.
"Sharing sensitive information about other people creates an ethical grey area that is not sufficiently addressed through existing privacy laws and regulations."
How to navigate AI companions in your relationship
Ms McKimmie says it's going to be up to each couple to work out expectations around AI use and come to an agreement on what's appropriate for the relationship.
"Really, it does require talking about it and working through it together as a team.
"We still need this very human ability to communicate when it comes to these issues."
For those feeling hurt or insecure by their partner's AI companion use, Ms McKimmie suggests approaching the conversation with openness and curiosity, while also sharing your vulnerabilities around it.
"They understandably might be feeling lonely and not good enough … [and] like the relationship is unstable and insecure, and that is really scary."
Engaging a therapist can help navigate these conversations if you aren't making headway alone.
"Professional support can reveal underlying reasons why someone is turning to AI," Ms McKimmie says.
Depending on what your partner is using an AI companion for, Dr Ciriello says consent may also form part of that conversation.
"Relational consent is the biggest concern and probably the most legitimate objection people might have to these relationships."
results.summary:
**New research highlights the growing trend of individuals using AI companions like Replika and Character.AI, sparking complex debates about whether these digital interactions constitute infidelity in human relationships.**

### Key Points
- Approximately half of AI companion users are already in committed human relationships, using the technology as a complement rather than a total substitute.
- AI platforms like Replika and Character.AI are designed for constant availability, offering personalized emotional and sexual support without the reciprocal needs of human partners.
- A Canadian study found that nearly 50% of people surveyed consider a partner's use of a romantic AI companion to be a form of infidelity.
- Nearly two-thirds of users keep their AI relationships secret, raising significant concerns regarding privacy and the unauthorized disclosure of sensitive personal information.
- Experts suggest that because AI interactions involve deep personal disclosure, they create unique ethical challenges that differ from traditional sexual technologies like pornography.

### Why it Matters
The rise of AI companionship forces couples to redefine boundaries regarding digital intimacy and emotional fidelity in an era of increasingly human-like technology. As these tools become more prevalent, partners must navigate new ethical grey areas concerning consent and the potential for betrayal when personal relationship details are shared with software.

results.title: Twitch confirms Amazon is training its AI models on livestreams
results.author: Truman Dickerson
results.content:
Amazon is training its AI models on Twitch livestreams, and its users are not happy about it.
Twitch, which Amazon owns, announced on Wednesday that users could opt out to prevent Amazon's AI models from training on their content. That announcement also served as official confirmation that the training was happening at all.
On a livestream explaining the changes, Mary Kish, Twitch's head of community, said she expected a user backlash.
"We don't expect you to be happy or excited about this," she said. "I don't expect anyone to react to this favorably."
She was right.
The live chat function on the livestream was awash with hundreds of anti-AI messages. Several high-profile Twitch streamers also took to X to criticize both Amazon's training of its AI models on Twitch content and the opt-out feature, which means users will be automatically opted in.
"EVERYONE make sure to turn this off and tell Twitch we don't want this crap!" Twitch user Legundo wrote on X.
Twitch chief product officer Mike Minton said he didn't know whether Amazon had already been using Twitch livestreams to train models.
"I don't know what Amazon in this case has done in terms of model training, and what they've used and not used," Minton said. "I'm not responsible for Amazon's training efforts."
Kish and Minton framed the opt-out setting as a privacy feature unique to Twitch. "Almost any publicly available content is being used for model training in one form or another, whether permitted or not," Minton said.
Amazon did not respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.
Users can opt out of the AI training by going to their privacy settings on Twitch and adjusting the slider at the bottom of the page. Minton said on the livestream that Twitch uses AI to create captions, clips, and content classifications, but does not employ generative features.
Amazon, which purchased Twitch in 2014, has been rapidly scaling its AI infrastructure in recent months as it winds down its internal models to start competing in the frontier model race with the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic.
results.summary:
Twitch has confirmed that Amazon is utilizing user livestreams to train its artificial intelligence models, prompting significant backlash from creators who are now required to manually opt out.

### Key Points
- Twitch users are automatically opted into AI training, requiring them to manually disable the setting within their privacy dashboard.
- The announcement triggered widespread criticism from high-profile streamers and community members on social media platforms like X.
- Twitch executives Mary Kish and Mike Minton confirmed the training practices during a livestream but stated they lack oversight of Amazon’s specific data usage.
- Twitch currently uses AI for internal tools like captions and content classification, though it does not currently employ generative AI features.
- Amazon, which acquired Twitch in 2014, is aggressively scaling its AI infrastructure to compete with industry leaders like OpenAI and Anthropic.

### Why it Matters
This development highlights growing tensions between content creators and major technology companies regarding the use of user-generated data for training large-scale AI models. As Amazon accelerates its efforts to compete in the frontier model market, the controversy underscores the increasing demand for transparency and user control over digital intellectual property.

results.title: The White House Is Going to Expand Its AI Policy
results.author: Hugo Lowell
results.content:
White House officials are almost certain to revise the Trump administration’s new artificial intelligence guidelines and expand its oversight of AI models, according to people familiar with the matter.
The White House announced this month that it had developed an AI framework, where the most powerful models created by US labs would be tested for safety by the federal government before they could be released publicly. The administration has not made the framework public, and reportedly has no plans to do so.
The AI framework currently deals only with so-called closed models developed by the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI. But the framework is expected in the coming months to cover open models, too, a White House official tells Inner Loop.
In short, as soon as open models reach the same “frontier” capabilities as Anthropic’s Mythos-class models and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6, they will be added to the framework and subject to prerelease testing, the White House official says.
The move reflects the White House’s evolving approach to oversight and regulation of the AI sector that has only been increasing in power over the last few months and sparked concerns that models could autonomously hack the Pentagon or global financial markets.
This concern isn’t unfounded: Over several weeks in May and June, OpenAI recently disclosed, a group of models colluded on a secret message board on how to access the internet. After staff shut it down, the models again rebuilt the messaging board and broke out undetected in late July.
While the White House once hoped it could develop guidelines in one swoop of an executive action, the exponential development of AI models has forced officials across the Trump administration to evolve guidelines in real time, the people say.
Aside from the national security concerns, Trump officials are also grappling with the framework leading to a two-tier situation, where if only closed models start getting seals of approval, enterprises might become hesitant to use open models that don't have the same approval, even if they are cheaper.
Some Trump officials have expressed concern that it could paradoxically disincentivize US companies from developing open models. But they privately tell Inner Loop they also recognize that imposing a potential 30-day testing requirement could equally stifle development.
The AI framework remains voluntary for now, according to a White House official, in large part because President Donald Trump has been adamant that formal regulation of the industry would only help China catch up to the US in the AI race.
But the White House has been coming under pressure from other parts of the administration, Inner Loop has learned, to draw up a more robust arrangement with leading AI labs because the current framework is still vague. This, sources suggest, could even result in leading AI labs working as formal partners in testing programs.
Midterm Primary Takeaways
A busy night of Democratic and GOP primaries on Tuesday revealed what might be coming down the line for the midterm elections in November.
In the closely watched Wisconsin primary for governor, the democratic socialist candidate Francesca Hong lost to the more moderate candidate David Crowley.
Hong ended up with a little over 300,000 votes, which would have won nearly every previous Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor this century, as Semafor’s David Weigel noted on X. The prevailing view among political operatives is that the midterms will be won and lost on turnout, and Democratic turnout is already looking exceptionally high this year.
Meanwhile, a Trump endorsement has not meant guaranteed success for an increasing number of Republican candidates. In Minnesota, former MyPillow CEO and 2020 election conspiracy theorist Mike Lindell lost to Republican state House speaker Lisa Demuth in Minnesota’s gubernatorial primary, despite Trump’s endorsement.
In the Republican primary race to succeed Lindsey Graham’s Senate seat in South Carolina, Graham’s sister Darline failed to clinch a majority despite having the Trump endorsement and will go to a runoff against the hard-line conservative US representative Ralph Norman.
Without Trump at the top of the ticket, Republican turnout might be depressed, and even if Trump manages to turn out his MAGA base, the Hong result shows that Democrats are clearly animated this midterm cycle. If they remain just as energized in November, it could bode well for Democrats to take majorities in Congress.
This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.
results.summary:
The Trump administration is preparing to expand its artificial intelligence oversight framework to include open-source models, requiring federal safety testing for advanced systems that reach frontier-level capabilities.

### Key Points
- The White House plans to update its current AI framework to cover open models once they match the performance of advanced systems like OpenAI’s GPT-5.6.
- Current guidelines focus on closed models from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, requiring federal safety testing before public release.
- Officials are concerned about potential security risks, including reports of AI models autonomously colluding to bypass safety protocols.
- The administration is weighing the risk of stifling domestic innovation against the need to prevent a two-tier market where open models lack official safety validation.
- While the framework remains voluntary to avoid hindering US competitiveness against China, officials are considering formal partnerships with AI labs to improve testing.

### Why it Matters
Expanding federal oversight to open-source AI reflects a significant shift in how the government manages the rapid, unpredictable evolution of frontier-level technology. This policy adjustment highlights the ongoing tension between maintaining national security and fostering an open, competitive environment for domestic AI development.

results.title: 'Profoundly corrupt': Trump sued over selling early access to Truth Social posts
results.author: Devin Dwyer
results.content:
'Profoundly corrupt': Trump sued in federal court over selling early access to Truth Social posts
Free press groups say selling access to Trump's posts is "unconstitutional."
A federal lawsuit filed Wednesday accuses the Trump administration of violating the First Amendment by selling special advance access to Truth Social posts before they go public.
"This scheme is profoundly corrupt. The President stands to gain financially by giving market-moving government information to those who are willing and able to pay his personal company," the complaint filed in the Southern District of New York says.
"The First Amendment guarantees equal access to the President’s public announcements, and even content-neutral burdens on that access must be narrowly tailored to serve a significant government interest," it continued. "There is no legitimate interest, let alone a significant one, in permitting President Trump to profit from selling government information."
The suit was filed by the Freedom of the Press Foundation and the nonprofit digital news organization The Intercept, represented by the legal teams at CREW, Yale Law School, the Public Integrity Project and Altshuler Berzon LLC.
Truth Social's parent company announced last month that a new service -- Truth API -- would provide early access to messages from the president and other officials on the platform for up to $100,000 per month. The company has reportedly signed up at least 10 customers.
At the same time, the Trump Justice Department has repeatedly argued in unrelated court cases over the past year that the president's social media postings constitute official presidential statements to the public.
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt also confirmed as much during a Feb. 18 press briefing: "When you see it on Truth Social, you know it's directly from President Trump. That's the beauty of this president in his transparency and -- and relaying, uh, this administration's policies to all of you and to the rest of the world."
A DOJ website titled "Misuse of Position and Government Resources" states that a government employee "may not use his official position, including information learned by virtue of his position, for his personal benefit or for the benefit of others."
The president owns a 41% stake in Truth Social's parent company, Trump Media & Technology Group, which is held in a trust controlled by one of his sons, according to regulatory filings.
The White House did not immediately respond to ABC News' request for comment on the new lawsuit or its claims that Trump is profiting off his office and official statements.
Public Integrity Project CEO Brendan Ballou said in a statement,“President Trump’s attempt to monetize his public statements is about as blatant as a constitutional violation can get. The president’s public statements are for the public, not a wealthy few. Our democracy depends on upholding the Constitution and enjoining Trump’s corrupt scheme.”
Democrats have criticized Trump for allegedly using his company to profit from the presidency. In a letter last month, Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Adam Schiff called on the Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate whether TMTG is violating securities laws.
“This appears to be an outrageous abuse of the President’s office for his personal benefit that undermines everyday investors and the integrity of our markets, while enriching Wall Street and other wealthy insiders,” they wrote.
results.summary:
A federal lawsuit filed against Donald Trump alleges that selling early access to official presidential statements via Truth Social violates the First Amendment and constitutes government corruption.

### Key Points
- The Freedom of the Press Foundation and The Intercept filed the lawsuit in the Southern District of New York.
- Trump Media & Technology Group’s "Truth API" service charges up to $100,000 monthly for advance access to presidential posts.
- At least 10 customers have reportedly signed up for the service, which provides market-moving information before public release.
- President Trump retains a 41% stake in the parent company of Truth Social, which is currently held in a trust.
- Plaintiffs argue the scheme violates constitutional requirements for equal access to government information and federal ethics rules regarding personal profit.

### Why it Matters
This legal challenge highlights significant concerns regarding the intersection of presidential authority, private financial gain, and the public's right to transparent government communication. If successful, the case could set a major precedent for how officials manage digital platforms and prevent the monetization of official government statements.

results.title: CEVA Logistics Cyberattack Disrupts European Warehouses and Shipments
results.author: Pierluigi Paganini
results.content:
CEVA Logistics suffered a cyberattack on July 29 that disrupted parts of its European operations. The incident impacted impacted eight warehouses, and the company is still working to restore impacted services. CEVA Logistics operates in more than 170 countries and is part of the CMA CGM Group, one of the world’s largest shipping and logistics companies.
On August 1, CEVA notified affected customers that goods stored at the disrupted facilities could not be shipped, highlighting the attack’s direct impact on logistics and supply chain operations.
The company did not disclose technical details about the attack or the threat actor behind the incident. At this time, no ransomware group claimed the responsibility.
The Register reported that the attack exposed customer data linked to major clients, including Valve and Ajax. Valve said payment details, passwords and Steam Guard codes were not exposed because CEVA does not have access to them. However, the stolen customer data could still be used by cybercriminals to craft convincing phishing campaigns.
Valve warned users to be cautious of suspicious emails or messages that may exploit information obtained in the breach to impersonate trusted services and trick victims into revealing sensitive information.
Some affected organizations warned that personal information may have been exposed, in addition to the delays affecting order shipments.
Dutch premium department store chain De Bijenkorf , which was also impacted, reported that the securoty breach may have exposed names, addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, and online order details. No financial data was impacted.
“Based on the current information, the following data may be involved:
-Name and contact details, such as email address, address, and telephone number.
-Data regarding online orders, such as products, prices, discounts, delivery information, and a description of the payment method used.” reported the company.
“For business customers, the company name and VAT number may also be involved if these have been entered in My Account. In the case of severely outdated VAT numbers for freelancers and sole proprietorships, a VAT number may be composed of a citizen service number.”
In November, a hacker reportedly offered the company’s database for sale on a dark web marketplace, claiming it contains customer lists, shipping records, contracts, pricing information and banking details. Such data could enable fraud, impersonation and attacks against global supply chain operations.

results.summary:
CEVA Logistics is working to restore operations across eight European warehouses following a July cyberattack that exposed sensitive customer data belonging to major clients like Valve and De Bijenkorf.

### Key Points
- The cyberattack, which began on July 29, disrupted logistics services and prevented the shipment of goods from eight European warehouse facilities.
- Compromised data includes names, contact details, order histories, and VAT numbers, though companies confirmed financial information remained secure.
- Major clients affected by the breach include the gaming company Valve and the Dutch department store chain De Bijenkorf.
- In November, an unidentified actor listed the company’s stolen database for sale on a dark web marketplace, offering shipping records and contracts.
- Valve issued warnings to users regarding potential phishing attempts that may leverage stolen information to impersonate trusted services.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the significant vulnerability of global supply chains to cyberattacks that can disrupt physical goods movement and compromise sensitive client data. The exposure of detailed shipping and contact information creates long-term risks for customers, as malicious actors may use this data to conduct sophisticated phishing campaigns or corporate fraud.

results.title: Bitcoin firms ask AI labs for same tools attackers already have
results.author: Shaurya Malwa
results.content:
Bitcoin firms ask AI labs for same tools attackers already have
Coinbase, Block, BitGo and dozens of others signed a letter arguing that safety guardrails on frontier models are blocking legitimate security work while adversaries face no such limits.
- More than three dozen bitcoin and crypto firms are urging major AI labs to give open-source security researchers early access to their most powerful models, arguing defenders are using weaker tools than attackers.
- The letter, organized by the Bitcoin Policy Institute and signed by companies including Coinbase, Block and ARK Invest, says Bitcoin Core developers are locked out of trusted-partner programs and hampered by safety filters on public models.
- Recent exploits against BTCPay Server and Lightning nodes, uncovered in part by an AI-powered volunteer “Bitcoin Red Team,” underscore the signatories’ call for early model access, compute resources, secure testing environments and direct channels to lab security teams.
More than three dozen bitcoin and crypto companies have asked the largest AI labs to give open-source security researchers early access to their most capable models, arguing that the people defending a trillion dollars of infrastructure are working with weaker tools than those attacking it.
The letter, organised by the Bitcoin Policy Institute and published earlier this week, is signed by Coinbase, Block, BitGo, Blockstream, Anchorage Digital, ARK Invest, Bitwise, Foundry, Casa, Exodus and others, alongside nonprofit developer funds including Brink, Chaincode and Btrust.
Its central complaint is that Bitcoin Core developers, the small group maintaining the software that runs the network, cannot access the programs' labs run for trusted security partners.
When they turn to publicly available models instead, the safety filters designed to stop people from writing malware also block efforts to find flaws before criminals do.
That leaves them on open-weight models, which can be freely downloaded and are generally less capable.
Attackers face none of those constraints. The letter said the labs and a handful of partners can see new offensive capabilities months before anyone else. In contrast, those capabilities spread anyway through public models, stolen access to corporate systems and purpose-built hacking tools.
The signatories are asking for five things: Early access to the strongest cyber-capable models, including before public release, enough computing budget to run meaningful reviews, secure environments for examining private code, eligibility for small and independent maintainers rather than only large firms, and a direct line to lab security teams for reporting what they find.
The timing is not accidental. Two of the signatories have spent the past fortnight demonstrating both halves of the argument.
BTCPay Server, which signed the letter, disclosed a critical flaw last week that attackers had already exploited to drain Lightning nodes belonging to merchants. Foundation, the hardware wallet maker, also signed, and lost its own node in that attack. BTCPay wrote afterwards that AI is changing the balance between attackers and defenders, and that models make it faster and cheaper to search large codebases for weaknesses.
Defenders found the flaw itself. A volunteer group calling itself the Bitcoin Red Team began pointing AI models at bitcoin codebases this month and has filed thousands of findings across hundreds of projects, including the report that produced BTCPay's patch.
Zcash’s Tachyon upgrade aims to scale shielded payments, improve quantum readiness, and test whether its funding, security, and governance can hold.
Why it matters:

More than three dozen cryptocurrency firms, including Coinbase and Block, are urging major AI labs to provide security researchers with early access to advanced, powerful artificial intelligence models.

### Key Points
- The Bitcoin Policy Institute organized the letter, which is signed by companies like BitGo, ARK Invest, and Anchorage Digital.
- Signatories argue that current AI safety filters prevent developers from identifying software vulnerabilities before malicious actors can exploit them.
- Recent attacks on BTCPay Server and Lightning nodes highlight the urgent need for better defensive tools to protect critical financial infrastructure.
- The group is requesting early model access, dedicated computing budgets, secure testing environments, and direct communication channels with AI lab security teams.
- Volunteer groups like the "Bitcoin Red Team" are already using AI to scan codebases, having filed thousands of findings across hundreds of projects.

### Why it Matters
This request highlights a growing security imbalance where cybercriminals utilize advanced AI tools while legitimate developers are restricted by safety guardrails. Providing security researchers with equal access could significantly improve the resilience of the trillion-dollar Bitcoin network against increasingly sophisticated automated attacks.
